# fossick


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

`fossick` gets text from the web and puts it into Python programs. You
can give it a search query, a URL, an arXiv id, a YouTube link, a GitHub
repository, or a local file. It returns markdown that a person or a
language model can read. AI agents can use it to look up information.
Its functions return plain data such as strings, lists, and
dictionaries. You can print this data or pass it to a model.

[<code>search</code>](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/search.html#search)
sends a query to several search engines at once. It merges their answers
into one ranked list.
[`read`](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/core.html#read) takes one
target and returns its text.
[<code>fetch</code>](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/core.html#fetch)
downloads a page.
[`to_md`](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/core.html#to_md)
converts its HTML to markdown. Some sites refuse downloads from scripts.
[<code>fetch</code>](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/core.html#fetch)
can also load a page in a headless browser, a stealth browser, or a copy
of Chrome where you are logged in.
[`cdp_connect`](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/cdp.html#cdp_connect)
drives that Chrome for pages that need clicks or typing. You can also
use these functions from the shell with the `fossick` command. Agents
can call them through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server.

## Install

``` sh
uv add fossick
```

Search and plain downloads need nothing else. JavaScript rendering, the
stealth fetcher, and
[`google`](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/search.html#google) use
a headless browser through
[scrapling](https://github.com/D4Vinci/Scrapling). If these calls raise
[`BrowserUnavailable`](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/core.html#browserunavailable),
run `scrapling install` to download its browsers. The browser automation
in `fossick.cdp` drives your installed Google Chrome.

## Quick start

These three calls cover most uses.
[<code>search</code>](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/search.html#search)
returns a list of results. Each result is a dictionary with the page
`title`, its URL in `href`, and a snippet in `body`. `score` is the
merged ranking score. `engines` lists the search engines that returned
the page. `method='flashrank'` reorders results with a small relevance
model. This method needs `pip install flashrank`. Without `method`,
[`search`](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/cli.html#search) keeps
the merged order.

``` python
results = search('koshas github fts semantic code graph', method='flashrank', n=5)
for r in results: print(r['score'], r['engines'], r['title'], r['href'])
```

## One function for every source

Use [`read`](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/core.html#read) when
you have a target and want its text.
[`read`](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/core.html#read) first
calls
[`what_is`](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/core.html#what_is) to
classify the target. The result is the name of a reader:

- `dir` for a local folder
- `file` for a local file
- `arxiv` for an arXiv URL or id
- `youtube` for a YouTube link
- `github` for a repository
- `ghfile` for a file on GitHub
- `pdf` for a URL that ends in `.pdf` or `/pdf`
- `web` for any other http or https URL

A path that exists on disk wins over every URL rule.

[`read`](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/core.html#read) returns
the same seven fields for every supported target:

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>field</th>
<th>holds</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>ok</code></td>
<td>True when the reader produced content</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>kind</code></td>
<td>the reader used, one of the names above</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>title</code></td>
<td>the title, or the first heading of the text</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>source</code></td>
<td>the URL, or the absolute path of a local file</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>text</code></td>
<td>the content as markdown</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>skipped</code></td>
<td>why nothing was read, when <code>ok</code> is False</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>meta</code></td>
<td>details from that reader, such as the authors of a paper or the HTTP
status of a page, and the time it was read</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

Here [`read`](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/core.html#read)
opens this repository’s own README:

``` python
target = str(repo_root()/'README.md')
assert what_is(target) == 'file'
result = read(target)
assert sorted(result) == ['kind', 'meta', 'ok', 'skipped', 'source', 'text', 'title']
assert (result.ok, result.kind, result.title) == (True, 'file', 'fossick')
assert '# fossick' in result.text and result.skipped is None
result.kind, result.title, result.ok
```

A folder or GitHub repository contains multiple files.
[`read`](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/core.html#read) does not
combine them into one document. It returns `ok=True` with empty `text`
and the local path in `meta['path']`. You choose which files to open.
For a GitHub repository, that path is a fresh clone in `fossick`’s
cache. With `pages=True`, a PDF returns a list of `(page_index, text)`
pairs. Page indexes start at 0.

Sometimes a recognised target produces no content. A site can serve a
bot check instead of the page. A YouTube video can have no English
captions. A URL that looks like a PDF can return another file type.
[`read`](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/core.html#read) reports
these cases with `ok=False` and a reason in `skipped`. It does not
raise. It raises `ValueError` only when the target is not one of the
supported kinds.

## Common calls

``` python
search('query', n=10, region='auto', timelimit='y')   # results from the past year
research('query', n=5)                    # search, read the top pages, return a digest that cites them
fetch(url, auto=True)                     # try stronger download methods until one is not blocked
crawl(url, max_pages=5, same_domain=True) # follow links from url, staying on its site
google('query', n=10)                     # Google's own ranking, through the stealth browser
cdp = await cdp_connect(); pg = await cdp.open_page(url); print(await pg.snapshot())
```

From the shell: `fossick search "q"`, `fossick fetch URL --auto`,
`fossick research "q"`. For agents: `uvx fossick-mcp`, or
`fossick-mcp --http` to serve over HTTP instead of standard input and
output.

## A logged-in Chrome

Some pages are shown only to logged-in users. `fossick` uses a separate
copy of Chrome with remote debugging on port 9223. It uses the profile
at `~/.cache/fastcdp/cdp-chrome`.
[`cdp_connect`](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/cdp.html#cdp_connect)
starts Chrome the first time it is needed. Log in to a site once in that
window. The profile keeps the cookies. Later calls such as
`fetch(url, session=True)` use the logged-in session.
`fetch(url, auto=True)` and
[`read`](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/core.html#read) use this
Chrome when every other method is blocked.

To start Chrome by hand in a visible window, run
`await cdp_setup(headless=False)` and log in. The `fastcdp-setup`
command comes with the `fastcdp` dependency. It adds a launcher for the
same Chrome and profile to your applications.

## Untrusted URLs

`fetch(url, auto=True)` and
[`read`](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/core.html#read) can use
the logged-in Chrome on port 9223.
[`read`](https://vedicreader.github.io/fossick/core.html#read) uses
`auto=True` by default. This step starts Chrome when it is not running
and sends its cookies for the site. Use this mode only for URLs that you
chose. When a URL comes from a web page, document, or another person,
pass `auto=False`:

``` python
fetch(url, auto=False, max_bytes=20_000_000)   # plain HTTP only; stop after 20 MB
read(url, auto=False, max_bytes=20_000_000)    # also for PDFs, arXiv papers and GitHub files
```

With `auto=False`, `fossick` does not start a browser or connect to port
9223. This also applies to PDFs and redirects. The plain path refuses
private and local addresses. It connects only to the checked address. A
second DNS answer cannot send it to `127.0.0.1`. It checks each redirect
in the same way. `max_bytes` and `max_recv_speed` limit download size
and speed. Both limits are off by default. Through a proxy and in
browser paths, `fossick` checks only the first URL.

On a machine that inspects TLS traffic with its own root certificate,
`curl_cffi` does not trust that root. It does not use the system
keychain. A download then fails with
`curl: (60) ... unable to get local issuer certificate`. Set
`SSL_CERT_FILE` to a CA bundle file that holds the normal roots and the
inspection root. For example, run
`export SSL_CERT_FILE=~/Library/Java/macos-all-ca.pem`. `fossick` also
reads `CURL_CA_BUNDLE` and `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE`. You can pass
`ca_bundle=` on each call. Verification stays on.
